entries.title: The Ayyubid Dynasty
entries.summary: The Ayyubids, founded by Salahuddin (Saladin), ruled Egypt, Syria, and neighboring lands after ending Fatimid rule, and are famous for confronting the Crusader states.
entries.detailed_information: Salahuddin abolished the Fatimid caliphate in Egypt (1171), restored Sunni Abbasid allegiance, and unified large parts of Syria and Egypt. In 1187 he recaptured Jerusalem after the Battle of Hattin. The Third Crusade followed, ending in negotiated truces rather than permanent Crusader recovery of Jerusalem. After Salahuddin's death (1193), Ayyubid territories fragmented among relatives and were later replaced in Egypt by the Mamluks.
entries.location: Egypt, Syria, Yemen and adjacent regions at various times
entries.historical_significance: Central Muslim dynasty of the Crusades era; restored Jerusalem to Muslim rule in 1187.
related_questions: What happened at the Battle of Hattin?
entries.source: Ibn Shaddad, The Rare and Excellent History of Saladin

entries.title: Salahuddin Ayyubi (Saladin)
entries.summary: Salahuddin Ayyubi was the Kurdish Muslim commander and sultan who founded Ayyubid rule, defeated Crusaders at Hattin, and retook Jerusalem in 1187 CE.
entries.detailed_information: Rising in the service of Nur al-Din's orbit, Salahuddin became ruler of Egypt and later Syria. He is remembered in both Islamic and European historical memory — in the latter often for chivalry narratives, which should be treated carefully as literary constructions. After 1187, he faced the Third Crusade led by figures such as Richard I. He died in Damascus in 1193. After his death, his relatives divided the realm, weakening centralized Ayyubid power.
entries.historical_significance: Iconic leader of Muslim resistance during the Crusades and restorer of Jerusalem.

entries.title: Battle of Hattin
entries.summary: The Battle of Hattin (1187) was Salahuddin's decisive victory over Crusader forces, enabling the Muslim recovery of Jerusalem later that year.
entries.detailed_information: Crusader armies were defeated near the Horns of Hattin in a campaign shaped by heat, water access, and tactical encirclement according to classical accounts. The defeat crippled Crusader military capacity in the region and opened the path to Jerusalem's surrender to Salahuddin.
entries.location: Near the Horns of Hattin, Galilee
entries.historical_significance: Decisive military turning point of the Crusades in the Levant.
entries.source: Ibn Shaddad, The Rare and Excellent History of Saladin
